as_told: King Hiero of Syracuse asked Archimedes to find out whether a goldsmith had mixed silver into a gold crown. Archimedes stepped into his bath, saw the water rise, and understood that he could measure the crown's volume by the water it pushed aside. He ran home naked, shouting "Eureka!" ("I have found it!"), and solved the problem.
lesson: Great ideas come in a sudden flash when you step away from a hard problem and relax.
what_happened: No record from Archimedes' own time (he died in 212 BC) tells the story. The earliest telling found is by the Roman architect Vitruvius, in the preface to Book 9 of his work on architecture, written about 30-20 BC, more than 180 years later. Vitruvius tells the bath scene and the cry, and then says that Archimedes "is said" to have tested the crown by measuring overflowing water. In about 1586 Galileo wrote that this overflow method was too crude to be the method Archimedes really used, and he proposed a method with a balance instead.
false_part: No record from Archimedes' time shows that the bath, the cry or the overflow test happened; the story first appears about two centuries later.

earliest_telling.who: Vitruvius (M. H. Morgan's 1914 English translation; Latin text ed. F. Krohn)
earliest_telling.where: De architectura (The Ten Books on Architecture), Book 9, preface, sections 9-12
earliest_telling.quote: happened to go to the bath, and on getting into a tub observed that the more his body sank into it the more water ran out over the tub

original.what: Vitruvius' Latin text of the same passage. The cry is given in Greek. The overflow test that follows is introduced with 'dicitur' ('it is said'), so Vitruvius himself reports it as hearsay.
The same passage in English: the overflow test is reported as 'it is said'.
original.quote: Taking this as the beginning of his discovery, it is said that he made two masses of the same weight as the crown

lesson_verdict.why: A meta-analysis of incubation studies found a real but modest benefit from setting an unsolved problem aside for a while. The benefit depends on the kind of problem and on what people do during the break, so the lesson holds only in this limited form.

source.what: Sio, U. N. and Ormerod, T. C. (2009), 'Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review', Psychological Bulletin 135(1): 94-120
source.quote: The authors identified a positive incubation effect, with divergent thinking tasks benefiting

Project Gutenberg text of Morgan's Vitruvius translation (ebook 20239): site was down for maintenance (503); not used.
Web search led to the Perseus/Perseids text of Vitruvius 9.pr.9-12 in Latin (Krohn) and English (Morgan); saved both. This is the earliest telling found; no older Greek or Latin telling was found.
Galileo Project page at galileo.rice.edu on the hydrostatic balance (lead only): says the story comes from Vitruvius and that Galileo answered it in La Bilancetta.

Italian Wikisource text of Galileo's La Bilancetta: saved; Galileo calls the overflow method 'molto grossa e lontana dall'esquisitezza' (very crude and far from exact). It is a later doubt, not a record of the event.

Archimedes' own works: saved the archive.org full text of T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897), which includes On Floating Bodies (file sources/archimedes-bath/heath1897-works-of-archimedes_djvu.txt). Heath cites Vitruvius IX.3 for the bath story and names no older source. The note in it that links On Floating Bodies I.7 to the crown is Heath's own suggestion in square brackets, not Archimedes' text. Archimedes' text states the law of buoyancy but does not tell the crown story.
Searched for a correction by the teller: none exists, because Vitruvius is the only ancient source and gives no correction.
Lesson: web search for a meta-analysis of incubation effects; saved Sio and Ormerod (2009) from gwern.net.

Wayback Machine: no capture of the gwern.net copy of Sio and Ormerod (2009), and the save request was refused with 403; so its archive link is empty. The two Perseids pages were saved on 22 November 2026.
confidence_note: Vitruvius may have used an older Greek source that is now lost, so the story could be older than him, but no such source survives. Whether an overflow test could detect the silver is a separate question; Galileo doubted it, but that does not show the bath scene did not happen.
